name: Melatonin (topical)

lead: Melatonin is best known as a sleep hormone, but hair follicles make it and carry melatonin receptors. Topical melatonin solutions are applied to the scalp by people hoping to slow hair loss and get thicker hair.

It is proposed to prolong the follicle growth phase and reduce oxidative stress in the scalp. A 2023 review identified 11 human studies in 2,267 patients and reported that eight observed positive outcomes in androgenetic alopecia, mainly more hair growth, density and shaft thickness versus controls. A 2024 review noted that most hair studies did not clearly demonstrate efficacy.

paras: It is used as a scalp solution applied regularly, usually alongside other hair-loss routines. Trials ran for a few months.

Topical use is generally well tolerated, with possible scalp irritation, or drowsiness if enough is absorbed. Melatonin is over the counter in the United States but prescription-only in parts of Europe, and long-term topical safety data are limited.

angle.text: Topical melatonin is applied to the scalp for thicker hair. Follicles carry melatonin receptors, and melatonin is thought to support the growth phase and reduce oxidative stress. A 2023 review found eight of 11 human studies reported positive outcomes, though most hair studies did not clearly demonstrate efficacy.

lead: Melatonin is an indoleamine hormone best known for regulating the sleep-wake cycle. It was discovered in 1958 by Aaron Lerner and colleagues, who isolated it from bovine pineal gland as a substance that lightened frog skin [1]. It acts on MT1 and MT2 receptors and also works as an antioxidant [1]. Human skin and hair follicles express melatonin receptors and synthesise melatonin themselves, which is the rationale for applying it to the scalp [2][3].

Topical melatonin solutions have been studied for androgenetic alopecia and other hair-loss complaints. A 2023 review identified 11 human studies in 2,267 patients and reported that eight observed positive outcomes with topical melatonin in androgenetic alopecia, mainly increased hair growth, density and shaft thickness compared with controls [3]. A 2024 review of clinical studies of topical melatonin noted that studies of photoprotection were well designed, while most hair studies did not clearly demonstrate efficacy [4].

Topical melatonin has also been tested for sunburn protection, radiation dermatitis and wound healing [4][5][6][7]. A 2026 case series reported topical melatonin in hair graying and repigmentation [8].
infobox: Varies by country; supplement in the US, prescription in some jurisdictions

paras: For hair, topical melatonin is applied to the scalp as a solution aimed at androgenetic alopecia, as an alternative or addition to minoxidil and finasteride [3][9]. Reviews also discuss topical melatonin as an antiaging skin ingredient and as an antioxidant photoprotectant [10][4].

Oral melatonin is used for insomnia and circadian rhythm sleep disorders [1]. Topical melatonin has been studied in radiation dermatitis [6], oral and periodontal conditions [11][12][13], psoriasis in combination with rosuvastatin [14], and diabetic foot ulcers [7].

Hair loss: a 2012 review described one pharmacodynamic study and four clinical pre-post studies of topical melatonin in androgenetic alopecia or general hair loss, evaluated by standardised methods [9]. The 2023 review of 11 human studies reported positive outcomes in eight AGA studies, with improved hair growth (eight studies), density (four) and shaft thickness (two) compared with controls, and a particular concentration reported as effective [3]. The 2024 review concluded that most hair studies did not provide a clear demonstration of efficacy, in contrast to well-designed photoprotection trials [4]. These studies were generally small, short, and many were uncontrolled pre-post designs.
Hair graying: a 2026 case series letter reported on hair graying repigmentation with topical melatonin [8].

Skin: randomised trials found that topical melatonin, alone or with vitamins E and C, reduced ultraviolet-induced erythema, including a dose-dependent study [4][5][15]. A randomised trial of topical melatonin during breast radiotherapy examined quality of life [6]. A crossover trial studied cognitive parameters after a 12.5% cream in healthy volunteers [16].

Melatonin acts as an agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors and is an antioxidant and free-radical scavenger that also upregulates antioxidant enzymes [1]. For hair, proposed mechanisms include modulating follicle cycling and reducing scalp oxidative stress through receptor-mediated and receptor-independent actions [3][10]. Reviews of its protection against oxidative DNA damage and cell protection are available [17][18].

Topical use is reported as generally well tolerated in the reviewed trials, though long-term topical safety data are limited [4]. A trial of 12.5% cream examined effects on cognition in healthy volunteers [16].

Wikipedia describes melatonin as widely sold as a supplement, with regulation differing between countries [1]. Forum mentions of melatonin in the sources reviewed concern sleep or travel rather than scalp use.
